newsitem.title: INDIA: India sugar price rise to cut state subsidies.
newsitem.headline: India sugar price rise to cut state subsidies.

text.p: India's decision to raise domestic sugar prices will mean an annual saving of at least $125 million to the government on subsidies, senior industry officials said on Tuesday.

"The current subsidy burden which the government bears is around 12 billion rupees ($334 million)," Mohan Sadashiv Marathe, managing director of the National Federation of Co-operative Sugar Factories Ltd, told Reuters.
"After the hike, the subsidy amount will come down to around 7.5 billion ($209 million)," he added.
Yatin Wadhwana, a leading Delhi sugar exporter, said: "It is a good move on the part of the government because it was long overdue."
On Monday, India raised the price of retail sugar for sale through its public distribution system (PDS) to 10.50 rupees per kg from 9.05 rupees. The rise was effective the same day.
A Food Ministry statement said the issue price for PDS was fixed at 9.05 rupees in February 1994.
It said since then the minimum price of sugarcane paid to farmers had been raised three times without any corresponding increase in retail sugar prices.
"The hike was long overdue as the minimum sugarcane price had been hiked three times (since February 1994) but a subsequent raise in issue price of levy sugar had not taken place," Marathe said.
The issue price is the rate at which the government supplies sugar at subsidised prices to government shops for sale through its public rationing system.

India has abolished licences for many industries under an economic reforms programme that began in 1991, but it has kept sugar under the old system, which subsidises prices for consumers and protects producers.

Sugar supplies and pricing in India are controlled by the government. The mills supply 40 percent of their output as levy sugar at a subsidised rate for distribution among the public at controlled prices and sell the rest on the open market.

Marathe said the government currently pays private mills 8.77 rupees a kg for the sugar it buys as levy. But it was costing the government around 20 rupees a kg after adding transport and distribution charges, he said.
Industry officials said India consumes nearly 13 million tonnes of sugar a year out of which five million tonnes is distributed as levy sugar.
Marathe said considerable quantities of sugar supplied to government shops were being illegally diverted to the open market and sold at much higher prices.
"The hike in the controlled sugar prices will substantially reduce the levy sugar leak to the open market to be sold at a higher price," Marathe said.
Industry officials said the sugar industry continued to face liquidity problems because the levy price paid to them had not been increased for the 1996/97 (October-September) season.
Shanti Lal Jain, director general of Indian Sugar Mills Association, told Reuters the government had already bought around 400,000-500,000 tonnes of sugar from private mills in 1996/97 at old prices.
Marathe said a rise of 0.60-0.70 rupees per kg in the levy sugar price was likely.
"We expect the new levy price to be announced by the government in the next couple of weeks," Wadhwana said.
($1 = 35.9 rupees)
